learn.b: Ruby runs a file from top to bottom, with no main function needed. puts prints a value and then a new line. Files end in .rb and you run them with ruby file.rb.
learn.code: puts "Hello, world!"

learn.b: puts adds a new line after the output. print does not. p shows the value the way a programmer would write it, for example with quotes around text.
learn.code:
print "Hi "
puts "there"
p "quoted"
p 42

learn.b: A variable is created by assigning with =. There is no keyword and no type. Names use lowercase words joined by underscores (snake_case). Constants start with a capital letter.
learn.code:
age = 12
user_name = "Mia"
age = age + 1
PI_ISH = 3.14
puts age

learn.b: Every value in Ruby is an object with methods you call using a dot. Use .class to see the type, and # starts a comment.
learn.code:
puts 5.class
puts "hi".class
puts nil.class
# comments start with a hash

learn.b: Strings are written in single or double quotes. Join them with + or <<. length gives the number of characters and [] reads one, starting at 0.
learn.code:
s = "Ruby"
puts s.length
puts s[0]
puts s + "!"

learn.b: Inside double quotes, #{ } puts any Ruby expression into the text. Single quotes do not interpolate and do not read escapes like \n.
learn.code:
name = "Ana"
puts "Hi #{name}"
puts "2 + 2 = #{2 + 2}"
puts 'Hi #{name}'

learn.b: Common methods are upcase, downcase, capitalize, reverse, strip, include?, start_with?, sub, gsub and split. Methods ending in ? return true or false.
learn.code:
puts "ruby".upcase
puts "abc".reverse
puts "a-b".gsub("-", "+")
puts "hello".include?("ell")

learn.b: Most methods return a new string. Methods ending in ! change the original, such as upcase!. A string times a number repeats it, and gets reads typed input.
learn.code:
s = "hi"
puts s * 3
s.upcase!
puts s

learn.b: Ruby has Integer for whole numbers of any size and Float for decimals. Dividing two integers gives an integer, so 7 / 2 is 3. Make one of them a float to get 3.5.
learn.code:
puts 7 / 2
puts 7 / 2.0
puts 7 % 2
puts 2 ** 10

learn.b: to_i turns text into an integer, to_f into a float and to_s into a string. Convert before doing math on text.
learn.code:
puts "42".to_i + 1
puts 3.9.to_i
puts 5.to_s + "!"
puts "2.5".to_f

learn.b: Numbers have handy methods: round, floor, ceil, abs, even?, odd?, zero?, and divmod. Math has sqrt and more.
learn.code:
puts 3.14159.round(2)
puts 7.even?
puts -5.abs
puts Math.sqrt(16)

learn.b: Integers can repeat things: 3.times runs a block three times, 1.upto(3) counts up. rand gives a random number. Underscores can make big numbers readable.

learn.b: if runs code when a condition is true. Extra branches use elsif (note the spelling), and the whole thing ends with the keyword end. Only false and nil count as false, everything else is true, even 0.
learn.code:
age = 15
if age >= 18
  puts "adult"
elsif age >= 13
  puts "teen"
else
  puts "kid"
end

learn.b: unless is the opposite of if: it runs when the condition is false. It reads well for simple negatives, but do not use elsif with it.
learn.code:
logged_in = false
unless logged_in
  puts "please log in"
end

learn.b: A modifier form puts the condition after the code. The ternary operator ?: chooses between two values. Combine tests with &&, || and !.
learn.code:
puts "even" if 4.even?
puts "ok" unless false
age = 20
puts age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor"

learn.b: case compares one value against several options with when, and else catches the rest. A when can list many values or a range, and no break is needed.
learn.code:
day = 3
case day
when 1 then puts "Mon"
when 2, 3 then puts "Tue or Wed"
when 4..7 then puts "later"
else puts "?"
end

learn.b: while repeats while the condition is true, and until repeats while it is false. Both end with end. Change a variable inside, or the loop never stops.
learn.code:
i = 1
while i <= 3
  puts i
  i += 1
end

learn.b: 1..5 is a range that includes 5, and 1...5 stops before 5. Rubyists prefer each to go over items. The part between pipes is the loop variable.
learn.code:
(1..3).each do |i|
  puts i
end
5.times { |n| puts n }

learn.b: step jumps by a number, upto and downto count, and loop do repeats until you break. each_with_index gives the position too.
break leaves a loop at once. next skips to the next round. Ruby has no ++ operator, so use += 1.
learn.code:
(1..5).each do |i|
  next if i == 2
  break if i == 4
  puts i
end

learn.b: An array is an ordered list in square brackets. Items can be any type, and you read them by position starting at 0. Negative positions count from the end, so -1 is the last. %w[] makes an array of words.
learn.code:
fruits = ["apple", "pear"]
puts fruits[0]
puts fruits[-1]
words = %w[a b c]
puts words.length

learn.b: push or << adds at the end, pop removes the last, shift removes the first and unshift adds at the front. insert and delete work by value or position.
learn.code:
a = [1, 2]
a << 3
a.push(4)
a.pop
puts a.inspect

learn.b: first, last, length, include?, sort, reverse, uniq, sum, min, max and join work on arrays. join makes one string from the items.
learn.code:
n = [3, 1, 2]
puts n.sort.inspect
puts n.max
puts n.sum
puts n.join("-")

learn.b: map transforms every item, select keeps items that pass a test, and reject removes them. Each returns a new array. Blocks are written with braces or do and end.

learn.b: A hash stores key and value pairs. Symbols such as :name are the usual keys, and the short form name: "Ana" means the same. Read a value with [].
learn.code:
user = { name: "Ana", age: 12 }
puts user[:name]
user[:age] = 13
puts user[:age]

learn.b: Reading a missing key gives nil. fetch raises an error unless you give a default. A Hash.new(0) gives 0 for missing keys, which is perfect for counting.
learn.code:
user = { name: "Ana" }
p user[:x]
puts user.fetch(:x, "none")
count = Hash.new(0)
count["a"] += 1
puts count["a"]

learn.b: each gives the key and value. keys, values and key? help you inspect a hash. delete removes a key and size counts pairs.
learn.code:
h = { a: 1, b: 2 }
h.each do |k, v|
  puts "#{k} = #{v}"
end
puts h.keys.inspect
puts h.key?(:a)

learn.b: map, select and sum work on hashes too. Symbols are cheap, unique names, while strings as keys are fine too. Hashes keep the order you added items.

learn.b: Use def, a name, optional parameters and end. The last expression is returned automatically, though you can write return. Names use snake_case.
learn.code:
def add(a, b)
  a + b
end
puts add(2, 3)

learn.b: A parameter can have a default with =. Keyword arguments end in a colon and are named in the call, which makes calls easy to read.
learn.code:
def greet(name, greeting = "Hello")
  "#{greeting}, #{name}"
end
puts greet("Sam")
def box(w: 1, h: 1)
  w * h
end
puts box(h: 5)

learn.b: Without return, a method gives back its last evaluated line. You can return several values as an array. A method with no value returns nil. Questions end in ? and dangerous methods end in !.
learn.code:
def min_max(a)
  return a.min, a.max
end
lo, hi = min_max([3, 1, 2])
puts lo
puts hi

learn.b: *args collects extra arguments into an array. Variables inside a method are local and not visible outside it. Parentheses on calls are optional, but they keep code clear.
learn.code:
def total(*nums)
  nums.sum
end
puts total(1, 2, 3)

learn.b: A block is a chunk of code passed to a method, written with braces or do and end. A method runs it with yield. Blocks can take parameters between pipes.
learn.code:
def twice
  yield
  yield
end
twice { puts "hi" }
def show
  yield 5
end
show { |n| puts n * 2 }

learn.b: A method can check whether a block was passed with block_given?. That lets one method work both with and without a block. Blocks are what each, map and select use.
learn.code:
def maybe
  if block_given?
    yield
  else
    puts "no block"
  end
end
maybe
maybe { puts "block" }

learn.b: A Proc saves a block in a variable so you can keep it and call it later with call. Proc.new and proc create one.
learn.code:
say = Proc.new { |name| puts "Hi #{name}" }
say.call("Ana")

learn.b: A lambda is a stricter proc made with lambda or the arrow ->. It checks the number of arguments, and return inside it only leaves the lambda. Call it with call, .() or [].
learn.code:
sq = ->(x) { x * x }
puts sq.call(4)
puts sq.(5)
puts sq[6]

learn.b: A class is a blueprint. initialize runs on Class.new, and instance variables start with @. attr_reader and attr_accessor make getters and setters. Create objects with new.
learn.code:
class Dog
  attr_reader :name
  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end
  def bark
    "#{@name} says woof"
  end
end
d = Dog.new("Rex")
puts d.bark

learn.b: A class can inherit with <, getting all its methods. Use super to call the parent's version. A class can have only one parent.
learn.code:
class Animal
  def sound
    "..."
  end
end
class Cat < Animal
  def sound
    "Meow"
  end
end
puts Cat.new.sound

learn.b: A module groups methods and constants, and cannot be instantiated. Use it as a namespace with ::, or mix it into a class with include to share behavior.
learn.code:
module Greet
  def hello
    "Hello from #{self.class}"
  end
end
class Bot
  include Greet
end
puts Bot.new.hello

learn.b: A gem is a package of Ruby code shared on rubygems.org. Install one with gem install name or list it in a Gemfile and run bundle install. Then load it with require.
learn.code:
# terminal: gem install colorize
require "json"
puts({ a: 1 }.to_json)
# Gemfile: gem "sinatra"
